clinicalPearls: Phosphoglycerate kinase deficiency is an X-linked recessive glycolytic enzymopathy caused by PGK1 variants, mainly affecting males
It produces a variable combination of chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia, a metabolic myopathy with exercise intolerance and recurrent rhabdomyolysis, and central nervous system involvement
CNS features can include intellectual disability, seizures, and stroke-like episodes, and any given patient may have one, two, or all three components
Because PGK is a core glycolytic enzyme, its deficiency impairs energy production in erythrocytes, muscle, and neurones, explaining the multisystem phenotype
Exertional myoglobinuria can precipitate acute kidney injury and requires prompt recognition
Diagnosis rests on reduced PGK enzyme activity in red cells or muscle and confirmatory PGK1 genetic testing
Management is supportive: avoiding strenuous exertion and rhabdomyolysis triggers, transfusion or folate support for haemolysis, and seizure control as needed
reference.pathophysiology: Phosphoglycerate kinase catalyses an ATP-generating step of glycolysis, converting 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to 3-phosphoglycerate. PGK1 is X-linked and expressed in almost all tissues, so deficiency impairs glycolytic ATP production broadly. In erythrocytes, which depend on glycolysis for energy, reduced ATP shortens red-cell survival and causes chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia. In skeletal muscle, impaired glycolysis limits energy during anaerobic exertion, producing exercise intolerance, cramps, and rhabdomyolysis. In the brain, deficient energy metabolism underlies the intellectual impairment, seizures, and stroke-like episodes seen in some patients. The particular combination of features varies with the specific variant.
additionalDifferentials: Other glycolytic enzymopathies (e.g. pyruvate kinase, phosphofructokinase deficiency)
McArdle disease and other muscle glycogenoses
Other causes of chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia (e.g. G6PD deficiency)
Mitochondrial disorders with myopathy and stroke-like episodes
Fatty acid oxidation defects causing rhabdomyolysis
additionalInvestigations: Phosphoglycerate kinase enzyme activity assay in erythrocytes and/or muscle
Full blood count, reticulocytes, and haemolysis markers (bilirubin, LDH, haptoglobin)
Creatine kinase, with urine myoglobin during episodes of exertional muscle injury
Brain MRI and EEG where CNS features are present
redFlags: Acute rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria threatening acute kidney injury
Severe anaemia requiring transfusion or causing cardiovascular compromise
Stroke-like episodes or new focal neurological deficit
Status epilepticus or rapid neurological deterioration
reference.prognosis: The prognosis varies widely with phenotype; isolated haemolysis or myopathy may be manageable with supportive care, whereas significant CNS involvement carries a worse outlook, and recurrent rhabdomyolysis poses ongoing renal risk.
pitfalls: Attributing exertional muscle symptoms to a glycogenosis without considering a glycolytic enzymopathy
Missing the diagnosis in a boy with unexplained non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia
Failing to counsel on avoidance of rhabdomyolysis triggers and prompt management of myoglobinuria
Overlooking the X-linked inheritance in genetic counselling of the family
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
management: Avoid strenuous anaerobic exertion and other triggers of rhabdomyolysis and pace physical activity
Treat exertional rhabdomyolysis with vigorous intravenous hydration and manage resulting acute kidney injury, with renal replacement if needed
Support the chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia with folate supplementation and transfusion during crises, considering splenectomy in selected severe cases
Manage central nervous system involvement with anticonvulsants and neurorehabilitation for seizures, stroke-like episodes and developmental impairment
Monitor renal function, creatine kinase and haemolysis markers, and check urine myoglobin during exertional episodes
Offer genetic counselling for this X-linked disorder with carrier testing of female relatives
Coordinate care across haematology, metabolic medicine and neurology
